title: The Meiji Restoration
subtitle: How Japan modernised · 1853 – 1912
subject: meiji-restoration
intro: In 1853 American warships forced open a Japan that had kept the world at arm's length for two centuries. The shock brought down the Tokugawa shogunate, and in 1868 a group of young samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū restored power to the teenage Emperor Meiji. In barely forty years they abolished the feudal domains and the samurai class, built railways, factories, schools and a conscript army, adopted a constitution and parliament, overturned the unequal treaties, and defeated both China and Russia — turning Japan into the first non-Western industrial great power, and an empire.

chapters.title: The shock
chapters.text: For over 200 years Japan had kept almost all foreigners out. A military ruler, the shogun, governed from Edo, while the emperor in Kyoto was only a figurehead. In 1853 American steam warships sailed into Edo Bay and demanded that Japan open its ports. Japan had no navy to resist, so the shogun signed treaties that let foreigners trade on their terms and live outside Japanese law.
chapters.why: The shogun's whole claim to power was that he protected Japan. Giving in to foreigners made him look weak.

chapters.title: The crisis
chapters.text: Angry young samurai rallied around the emperor with the slogan 'revere the emperor, expel the barbarians'. They murdered officials and attacked foreigners. But when British and other warships shelled Kagoshima and Shimonoseki, the domains of Satsuma and Chōshū learned they could not beat the West with swords. They bought Western guns instead, and secretly allied against the shogun.
chapters.why: The rebels realised the answer was not to drive the West out, but to copy its strength.

chapters.title: The revolution
chapters.text: The last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, handed power back to the emperor. In January 1868 Satsuma and Chōshū troops declared imperial rule restored in the name of the 15-year-old Emperor Meiji. A short civil war, the Boshin War, defeated the shogun's supporters, and the new government promised in the Charter Oath to 'seek knowledge throughout the world'.
chapters.why: Power passed from the shogun to a small group of young reformers ruling in the emperor's name.

chapters.title: Clearing away the old order
chapters.text: In a few years the reformers abolished the 260 feudal domains and replaced them with prefectures run from Tokyo. They ended the privileges of the samurai and built an army of ordinary conscripts. Some samurai fought back. In 1877 Saigō Takamori, a hero of 1868, led the Satsuma Rebellion and was defeated by the new peasant army.
chapters.why: Japan went from a patchwork of lords to one centralised nation in under ten years.

chapters.title: Building a modern country
chapters.text: Japan's leaders toured America and Europe for almost two years to see how they worked. Back home they hired foreign experts and built railways, telegraphs, silk mills and schools for every child. In 1889 Japan adopted Asia's first modern constitution, and an elected parliament met in 1890.
chapters.why: Japan borrowed selectively: a German-style constitution, a British-style navy, and Western science, schools and banks.

chapters.title: A world power
chapters.text: Japan's new army and navy beat China in 1894–95 and then, to the world's surprise, Russia in 1904–05. The Western powers gave up the unequal treaties, and Britain became Japan's ally. Japan also became a colonial power itself, taking Taiwan and Korea. When Emperor Meiji died in 1912, Japan was an industrial great power.
chapters.why: In 59 years Japan went from being forced open to standing among the great powers. It was the first non-Western country to do so, at a heavy cost to its neighbours.

rows: Who rules
The shogun, a military ruler in Edo. The emperor is a figurehead in Kyoto.
Ministers rule in the emperor's name, under a constitution with a parliament.
The country
About 260 domains, each run by its own lord (daimyo).
One nation of prefectures, governed from Tokyo.
Society
Fixed classes. Only samurai may carry swords.
Samurai privileges abolished. Anyone can choose any job.
Army
Samurai with swords and old muskets. No real navy.
A conscript army and a modern navy that has beaten Russia.
Travel
On foot, on horseback or by palanquin.
Railways, steamships and the telegraph link the country.
School
Temple schools for some children.
Primary school for every child; almost all attend.
Economy
Mostly rice farming.
Silk mills, steelworks, banks and big business groups.
The world
Closed country: only the Dutch and Chinese may trade, at Nagasaki.
Equal treaties with the West, an ally of Britain, and an empire of its own.

events.title: Perry's 'Black Ships' at Uraga
events.summary: Commodore Matthew Perry steams into Edo Bay with four warships and delivers a letter from the American president demanding that Japan open its ports. After two centuries of sakoku the shogunate has no navy to resist him and, unusually, asks the daimyo and the court for advice — weakening its own authority.

events.title: Tokugawa Iesada becomes shogun
events.summary: The sickly Iesada succeeds his father, who died days after Perry left. Real power lies with the senior councillors, and the question of who will succeed the childless Iesada splits the shogunate.

events.title: Convention of Kanagawa
events.summary: Perry returns with a larger fleet and the shogunate signs Japan's first modern treaty. Shimoda and Hakodate open to American ships for supplies, and an American consul may live in Japan. Britain, Russia and the Netherlands soon win similar terms.

events.title: Harris Treaty and the 'unequal treaties'
events.summary: Townsend Harris wins a full commercial treaty: Yokohama, Nagasaki and other ports open to trade, foreigners get extraterritoriality, and Japan loses control of its own tariffs. Ii Naosuke signs without the consent of Emperor Kōmei, and four European powers follow with the same terms. Revising these unequal treaties becomes the central goal of Japanese diplomacy for the next fifty years.
events.wiki: Treaty of Amity and Commerce (United States–Japan)

events.title: Iemochi named shogun
events.summary: Iesada dies and Ii Naosuke installs the twelve-year-old Tokugawa Iemochi, defeating the faction that wanted the able Hitotsubashi Yoshinobu.

events.title: Ansei Purge
events.summary: Ii Naosuke crushes critics of the treaties and of his choice of shogun. Lords are confined, courtiers dismissed and about a hundred people punished. The teacher Yoshida Shōin, whose pupils include Itō Hirobumi and Yamagata Aritomo, is executed in Edo in 1859.

events.title: Ii Naosuke assassinated at the Sakurada Gate
events.summary: Ronin from Mito and Satsuma cut down Ii Naosuke in the snow outside Edo Castle. The killing of the shogunate's strongman shows that its authority can be defied, and the cry of sonnō jōi — 'revere the emperor, expel the barbarians' — spreads among young samurai.

events.title: Namamugi Incident
events.summary: Satsuma retainers kill the British merchant Charles Richardson on the road near Yokohama for failing to give way to their lord's procession. Britain demands an indemnity from the shogunate and the punishment of the killers from Satsuma.

events.title: The Chōshū Five sail for London
events.summary: Even as Chōshū calls for expelling foreigners, it secretly sends five young samurai, among them Itō Hirobumi and Inoue Kaoru, to study at University College London. They return as convinced modernisers and later run Japan's government, railways, mint and engineering schools.

events.title: Chōshū fires on foreign ships at Shimonoseki
events.summary: Taking the court's order to expel the barbarians literally, Chōshū's batteries shell Western ships in the Shimonoseki Strait. In 1864 a British, French, Dutch and American fleet destroys the forts — teaching Chōshū that Japan must learn Western military technology before it can resist the West.

events.title: Royal Navy bombards Kagoshima
events.summary: When Satsuma refuses to hand over Richardson's killers, a British squadron shells Kagoshima. Satsuma pays up, but rather than resenting Britain it begins buying British ships and guns and sends students to Britain in 1865.

events.title: Kinmon Incident in Kyoto
events.summary: Chōshū troops try to seize the emperor's palace and are driven off by Aizu and Satsuma. The shogunate brands Chōshū an enemy of the court and sends a punitive army against it.

events.title: Satsuma–Chōshū Alliance
events.summary: Brokered by the Tosa ronin Sakamoto Ryōma, the old rivals Satsuma and Chōshū secretly agree to stand together against the shogunate. Saigō Takamori and Kido Takayoshi seal the pact that will overthrow the Tokugawa.

events.title: Second Chōshū expedition fails
events.summary: The shogunate's second army against Chōshū is beaten by Chōshū's modern, partly commoner rifle units while Satsuma refuses to help. When Shogun Iemochi dies in Osaka in August the campaign is called off — a humiliating defeat for the Tokugawa.

events.title: Tokugawa Yoshinobu, the last shogun
events.summary: Yoshinobu becomes the fifteenth Tokugawa shogun and launches French-assisted reforms of the army and government — too late to save the regime.

events.title: Death of Emperor Kōmei; Mutsuhito succeeds
events.summary: Kōmei, who hated foreigners but supported the shogunate, dies of smallpox at 35. His fourteen-year-old son Mutsuhito, the future Emperor Meiji, takes the throne on 13 February, and the anti-Tokugawa courtier Iwakura Tomomi returns to influence.

events.title: Yoshinobu returns power to the emperor
events.summary: Urged by Tosa, Yoshinobu formally hands his governing authority back to the court, hoping to lead a council of lords under the emperor. A month later Sakamoto Ryōma, who had drafted a plan for just such a council, is murdered in Kyoto.

events.title: Restoration of imperial rule
events.summary: Satsuma and allied troops seize the palace gates in Kyoto, and Iwakura Tomomi has the young emperor proclaim the restoration of direct imperial rule. The shogunate is abolished and Yoshinobu is ordered to give up his lands — the moment from which the Meiji Restoration is dated.

events.title: Battle of Toba–Fushimi; the Boshin War begins
events.summary: Tokugawa troops marching on Kyoto are routed by smaller Satsuma and Chōshū forces carrying the imperial banner. Yoshinobu flees to Edo by ship, and many domains go over to the new government.

events.title: The Charter Oath
events.summary: The emperor swears five principles before the court and lords: affairs decided by public discussion, all classes united, every person free to pursue a calling, 'evil customs of the past' abandoned, and 'knowledge sought throughout the world' to strengthen imperial rule. It becomes the founding charter of modern Japan.

events.title: Edo Castle surrenders without a fight
events.summary: Saigō Takamori and the shogunate's Katsu Kaishū negotiate the peaceful handover of Edo Castle, sparing a city of a million people from a battle.

events.title: Siege of Aizu
events.summary: The northern alliance's stronghold holds out for a month. The suicide of teenage samurai of the Byakkotai, who thought the castle had fallen, becomes a lasting symbol of loyalty.

events.title: The Meiji era is proclaimed
events.summary: The era name Meiji, 'enlightened rule', is adopted, and from now on each emperor will have just one era. Edo has already been renamed Tokyo, 'eastern capital', and the emperor moves into the former shogun's castle, which becomes the Imperial Palace.

events.title: Fall of Hakodate ends the Boshin War
events.summary: Admiral Enomoto Takeaki had sailed the shogunate fleet north and set up the Republic of Ezo, with French officers and Hijikata Toshizō of the Shinsengumi. It surrenders at Hakodate after Hijikata is killed, and Japan is united under the emperor. Enomoto is pardoned and later serves as a minister.

events.title: The domains return their registers
events.summary: Led by Satsuma, Chōshū, Tosa and Hizen, the daimyo hand their land and population registers to the emperor and are reappointed as governors. The court nobles and lords are merged into a single nobility, the kazoku, and ordinary samurai become shizoku.

events.title: Ezo becomes Hokkaido
events.summary: The northern island is renamed Hokkaido and a Colonisation Office is set up to settle it, often with former samurai as farmer-soldiers, at the expense of the Ainu.

events.title: National postal service
events.summary: Maejima Hisoka launches a government post between Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka on the British model, replacing private couriers; it covers the country within a few years.

events.title: The yen is introduced
events.summary: The New Currency Act replaces the confusing mix of domain and shogunate money with a decimal currency, the yen, minted at a new Osaka mint with British machinery.

events.title: Domains abolished, prefectures created
events.summary: With 10,000 Satsuma, Chōshū and Tosa troops at its back, the government abolishes the 260-odd feudal domains in a single decree and replaces them with prefectures run by governors from Tokyo. The former lords are pensioned off to the capital. In one stroke a feudal patchwork becomes a centralised state.

events.title: The Iwakura Mission
events.summary: Iwakura Tomomi leads nearly fifty officials — Ōkubo, Kido and Itō among them — and sixty students on a journey through the United States and Europe. They fail to revise the treaties but study factories, parliaments, schools and armies, and come home convinced that Japan must build its strength before it confronts the West.

events.title: Fukuzawa's An Encouragement of Learning
events.summary: Fukuzawa Yukichi, founder of Keiō Gijuku, opens with the line that 'heaven does not create one person above another'. His essays on independence and practical learning sell hundreds of thousands of copies and define the 'civilisation and enlightenment' movement.

events.title: Universal education ordered
events.summary: The Education System Order, modelled on France, aims at 'no community with an illiterate family'. Primary schools spread across the country; by 1905 almost all children of school age are enrolled.
events.wiki: Education in the Empire of Japan

events.title: Tomioka Silk Mill opens
events.summary: A model state factory with French machinery and engineers trains young women from across Japan in mechanised silk reeling. Raw silk becomes Japan's biggest export and pays for much of its industrialisation.

events.title: First railway, Shimbashi to Yokohama
events.summary: The emperor opens Japan's first railway, 29 km between Tokyo and the treaty port of Yokohama, built with British engineers and loans. Telegraph lines and lighthouses go up in the same years, much of it the work of foreign experts hired by the government.

events.title: Japan adopts the Western calendar
events.summary: The lunar calendar is dropped: the 3rd day of the 12th month of Meiji 5 becomes 1 January 1873. Western dress, haircuts, beef and newspapers become emblems of the new age.

events.title: Universal conscription
events.summary: Yamagata Aritomo's conscription law makes every man liable for three years' service regardless of class, ending the samurai's monopoly of arms. The new army, trained first on French and later German lines, is built from peasants.

events.title: First National Bank founded
events.summary: Shibusawa Eiichi, a former shogunate retainer, founds Japan's first modern bank. He goes on to help start some five hundred companies — railways, shipping, paper, textiles, insurance — and is called the father of Japanese capitalism.

events.title: Land Tax Reform
events.summary: Feudal rice dues are replaced by a cash tax of 3% on the assessed value of land, and farmers receive title deeds. The tax gives the state a steady income for its reforms, though protests force a cut to 2.5% in 1877.

events.title: The Korea debate splits the government
events.summary: While the Iwakura Mission was abroad, Saigō Takamori and Itagaki Taisuke planned to force Korea open, by war if needed. The returning Ōkubo and Iwakura insist that reform at home must come first; Saigō, Itagaki and Etō Shinpei resign.

events.title: Freedom and People's Rights Movement
events.summary: Itagaki Taisuke petitions for an elected assembly, launching a nationwide movement of political societies, newspapers and draft constitutions. It pushes the oligarchs to promise a constitution.

events.title: Saga Rebellion
events.summary: Etō Shinpei leads discontented samurai in Saga; the uprising is crushed within weeks and Etō is executed. It is the first of several samurai revolts.

events.title: Expedition to Taiwan
events.summary: After Ryukyuan sailors are killed by Taiwanese aborigines, Japan sends troops to Taiwan — its first overseas expedition. China pays an indemnity, implicitly accepting Japan's claim to the Ryukyus.

events.title: Treaty of Saint Petersburg
events.summary: Japan gives up its claims to Sakhalin in exchange for all of the Kuril Islands, fixing its northern border with Russia.

events.title: Japan forces Korea open
events.summary: After a naval clash off Ganghwa Island, Japan imposes on Korea the same kind of unequal treaty the West had imposed on Japan — ports, extraterritoriality and a denial of Chinese overlordship.

events.title: End of samurai privileges
events.summary: The Haitōrei edict bans the wearing of swords in public, and samurai stipends are converted into government bonds. The samurai class loses both its symbol and its income.

events.title: Satsuma Rebellion
events.summary: Saigō Takamori, the hero of the Restoration, leads some 40,000 Satsuma samurai against the government he helped create. The conscript army, supplied by steamship and telegraph, wins; Saigō dies at Shiroyama above Kagoshima. It is the last samurai uprising and proves the peasant army.

events.title: University of Tokyo founded
events.summary: Several government colleges merge into Japan's first modern university, staffed at first largely by foreign professors. In 1886 it becomes the Imperial University, training the country's bureaucrats.

events.title: Ōkubo Toshimichi assassinated
events.summary: The architect of the early Meiji state is killed in Tokyo by samurai who blame him for Saigō's death. With Kido dead of illness in 1877, leadership passes to younger men — Itō Hirobumi above all.

events.title: Ryukyu annexed as Okinawa Prefecture
events.summary: The Ryukyu Kingdom, which had paid tribute to both China and Japan, is abolished and its king removed to Tokyo.

events.title: Matsukata deflation and the Bank of Japan
events.summary: Finance Minister Matsukata Masayoshi cuts spending, sells off state factories to private firms and founds the Bank of Japan (1882). The sell-offs to Mitsui, Mitsubishi and others help create the zaibatsu.

events.title: A constitution promised by 1890
events.summary: Ōkuma Shigenobu, who wanted a British-style parliament soon, is forced out, and an imperial edict promises a constitution and an assembly by 1890. Itagaki founds the Liberal Party and Ōkuma the Constitutional Reform Party, Japan's first national parties.

events.title: Itō studies constitutions in Europe
events.summary: Itō Hirobumi spends over a year in Berlin and Vienna learning from Rudolf von Gneist and Lorenz von Stein, and decides on a Prussian-style constitution that keeps strong powers for the emperor.

events.title: The Rokumeikan opens
events.summary: A Western-style hall in Tokyo where the elite hold balls and banquets for foreign diplomats, meant to show Japan is 'civilised' enough for equal treaties. It becomes a symbol — mocked by many — of the rush to Westernise.

events.title: Cabinet system; Itō the first prime minister
events.summary: The old Council of State gives way to a European-style cabinet, and Itō Hirobumi becomes Japan's first prime minister. A modern civil service examination follows in 1887.

events.title: The Meiji Constitution
events.summary: The emperor grants Asia's first modern constitution as a gift to his subjects. It sets up a two-chamber Imperial Diet with an elected lower house and rights 'within the limits of law', but the emperor commands the army and navy and ministers answer to him, not to parliament.

events.title: Imperial Rescript on Education
events.summary: A short text on loyalty to the emperor, filial piety and duty to the state, read aloud in every school before the emperor's portrait. It shapes Japanese schooling until 1945.

events.title: The first Imperial Diet meets
events.summary: After the first general election in July — in which about 1% of the people, tax-paying men, could vote — the Diet opens. Its lower house soon uses its budget power to fight the oligarchs' cabinets.

events.title: Ōtsu Incident
events.summary: A police guard attacks the visiting Russian heir, Tsarevich Nicholas, with a sword. The government wants the attacker executed to appease Russia, but the Supreme Court insists on the law and gives life imprisonment — an early test of judicial independence.

events.title: Britain agrees to end extraterritoriality
events.summary: Foreign Minister Mutsu Munemitsu signs a treaty with Britain under which foreign consular courts will close in 1899; the other powers follow. Japan becomes the first non-Western country to escape the unequal treaties.
events.wiki: Anglo-Japanese Treaty of Commerce and Navigation

events.title: First Sino-Japanese War
events.summary: Japan and China fight over Korea. Japan's modern army and navy win on land at Pyongyang and at sea off the Yalu, then take Port Arthur and Weihaiwei. The world is stunned that the 'pupil' has crushed the old Asian giant.

events.title: Treaty of Shimonoseki and the Triple Intervention
events.summary: China recognises Korea's independence, cedes Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula and pays a huge indemnity. Six days later Russia, Germany and France force Japan to give back Liaodong — which Russia then leases for itself. The humiliation fuels a decade of naval and military build-up.

events.title: Japan joins the gold standard
events.summary: Using the Chinese indemnity as reserves, Matsukata puts the yen on gold, linking Japan to the London capital market and making foreign borrowing cheaper.

events.title: Extraterritoriality ends
events.summary: The revised treaties take effect: foreigners in Japan become subject to Japanese courts, and the treaty-port settlements are absorbed into Japanese cities.

events.title: Yawata Steel Works fires its first blast furnace
events.summary: The state steelworks in northern Kyushu, built partly with the Chinese indemnity and near the Chikuhō coalfields, begins producing iron and steel for rails, ships and guns. Heavy industry joins textiles as a pillar of the economy.

events.title: Anglo-Japanese Alliance
events.summary: Britain, the world's leading power, makes an alliance with Japan — its first with an Asian nation — aimed at Russia. If Japan fights one power, Britain stays neutral; if two, Britain joins.

events.title: Russo-Japanese War
events.summary: Japan strikes the Russian fleet at Port Arthur. General Nogi takes the fortress after a costly siege, the armies meet at Mukden in one of the largest battles before 1914, and Admiral Tōgō destroys Russia's Baltic Fleet at Tsushima in May 1905. An Asian nation has defeated a European great power, to wide excitement across Asia.

events.title: Battle of Tsushima
events.summary: Tōgō Heihachirō's fleet annihilates the Russian Baltic Fleet after its voyage halfway round the world, losing only three torpedo boats. It is one of the most complete naval victories in history.

events.title: Treaty of Portsmouth
events.summary: Mediated by Theodore Roosevelt, Russia hands Japan the Port Arthur lease, the southern Manchurian railway and southern Sakhalin, and recognises Japan's interests in Korea. There is no indemnity, and angry crowds riot in Tokyo's Hibiya Park.

events.title: Korea made a protectorate
events.summary: Japan takes control of Korea's foreign affairs, and Itō Hirobumi becomes the first Resident-General in Seoul.

events.title: Main railways nationalised
events.summary: The government buys up seventeen private lines to create a national network of about 7,000 km, and the South Manchuria Railway Company is formed to run the lines won from Russia.

events.title: Itō Hirobumi assassinated at Harbin
events.summary: The four-time prime minister and author of the constitution is shot on the station platform at Harbin by the Korean nationalist An Jung-geun.

events.title: Annexation of Korea
events.summary: Korea is annexed and ruled by a Japanese governor-general until 1945. With Taiwan, southern Sakhalin and Kwantung, Japan is now a colonial empire.

events.title: Tariff autonomy regained
events.summary: Foreign Minister Komura Jutarō signs a new treaty with the United States, followed by the other powers, restoring Japan's right to set its own customs duties. The last of the unequal treaties is gone — the goal set in 1858 is reached.

events.title: Death of Emperor Meiji
events.summary: The emperor dies at 59 after a reign that took Japan from feudal isolation to a constitutional, industrial great power with an empire. His son becomes the Taishō Emperor. On the day of the funeral in September, General Nogi Maresuke and his wife take their own lives to follow their lord.
